candidates.snippet:
Most next generation reactors will require fuels with high assay low enriched uranium (HALEU), which can significantly improve operational efficiency.
Nearly all of the more than 400 nuclear power reactors operating today use fuels made with low enriched uranium (LEU), containing no more than 5% of the fissile isotope uranium-235 (U-235).
HALEU, however, can be enriched up to 19.95% U-235.
“This could, in turn, increase the capacity factors of nuclear power plants.”
Capacity factor refers to the amount of electricity produced over a period of time relative to maximum output – an area where nuclear power already outperforms other energy sources by a wide margin.
Fuelling a nuclear future
HALEU can be produced through gas centrifuge enrichment, similar to LEU, or by downblending highly enriched uranium from legacy stockpiles. Enrichment to the HALEU range requires more uranium feedstock and separative work units — the mechanical effort needed to achieve the desired U-235 enrichment.
Nuclear fuel supplier Centrus Energy has already produced more than 900 kilograms of HALEU under a contract established through this programme, and several other companies have been selected to perform enrichment or reconversion work.
Addressing regulatory issues for sustainability
The greater enrichment of U-235 in HALEU also means that IAEA inspections would need to be more rigorous, as weapons-grade high enriched uranium could be produced with less feedstock and on a shorter timescale than LEU.
